title: "Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help"
hookLine: the hinge of the prayer: it turns from talking about God to talking to God, and it says one
last: YAWM AD-DIN — THE ACCOUNT IS IN KIND HANDS.

cards: Mecca, in the early years. A man named Bilal is enslaved there, and he has become a Muslim.
The early biographies say the man who owned him would drag him out into the noon heat, lay him on the burning sand, put a heavy rock on his chest, and tell him to give up his faith.
And Bilal, crushed under the stone, would say only one word, over and over. Ahad. Ahad.
One. One. He comes back in two days, as the voice of the call to prayer.

teach.h: THE PRAYER TURNS: ABOUT GOD, TO GOD.
teach.b: Verse five: “Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help.” In Arabic, iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in. Two things happen here.
First, the prayer turns around. For four verses it has talked about God: praise be to Him, the Merciful, the Owner of the Day. Now, suddenly, it talks to God.
You. In the conversation from day two, God's answer changes here too: this is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asked. Second, listen to the order of the Arabic.
It doesn't say we worship You. It says You, we worship. Putting You first makes it exclusive: only You, and only You for help.
Tawhid. The root is w-h-d, one; wahid is the number one. Tawhid means making one, affirming one.

It's the first half of the shahada from day nine: there is no god but God. It even has its own surah, four lines long, that opens: “Say: He is Allah, the One!” Here's why it matters on an ordinary Tuesday.
If God is one, everything else, however big it looms, isn't God. Your job, your phone, your fear, other people's opinion of you: real, and none of them ultimate.
One way to put tawhid: one center, instead of a dozen. That's what Bilal was saying under the rock. Not an argument.

how: Muslims say this verse in every unit of every prayer. Tawhid is the heart of Muslim belief, said in the shahada, and many Muslims raise the index finger of the right hand when they bear witness in the sitting part of the prayer.

games.q: what's inside verse five — tap the pairs.
p: one: Bilal's word under the rock

s: verse five still talks about God, like the verses before it
it turns and talks to God: Thee alone we worship.
"(alone)" is added in the English because of the Arabic word order
putting You first in Arabic makes it exclusive: You, and no one else.
al-Ikhlas, the four-line surah of oneness, is said to equal a third of the Qur'an
a hadith in Bukhari says so.

games.q: you're Bilal, on the burning sand with a rock on your chest. you're told to give up your faith. what do the early biographies say he says?
o: a long speech to his owner.
games.why: one word, over and over: ahad. he was later freed, and became the voice of the call to prayer.

practice: Sit still, and gather your attention into one place: the breath at the tip of your nose. Just that. When your mind splits off into a dozen places, the list, the text, the worry, notice it, and bring it back to the one breath.
Again and again. In the prayer, at the words of witness, many raise one finger of the right hand; you can rest one finger up while you sit, if you like. If you pray, let the word rest there: ahad.

wordCard.voice: Tawhid. The oneness of God, affirmed: You alone we worship, You alone we ask for help. Fifteenth word.

orig.note: Arabic: making one, affirming one. from w-h-d, one; wahid is the number one, ahad is Bilal's word.

carryVoice: Your line: one. One center, instead of a dozen things pulling at you. Day fifteen.
